newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian falls foul of communism and capitalism.
newsitem.headline: Albanian falls foul of communism and capitalism.

text.p: Namik Rroshi lives in a tiny hut that is even more cramped than the prison cell where he spent 19 years of his life under the old communist regime.
"I lost my freedom under the communists and now I've lost all my money with the new capitalists," says Rroshi, who is 60 but looks at least 10 years older.
Like thousands of other people across impoverished Albania, Rroshi ran afoul of the repressive communist regime of Enver Hoxha and was repeatedly thrown in jail for political dissent.
But five years after the birth of democracy, his hopes of a better life lie in ruins following the collapse last week of a pyramid investment scheme based in this southern Adriatic port.

Lured by promises of huge interest payments, Rroshi sold his house for $8,000 late last year and plunged all the proceeds into the fund. He moved into the hut and expected to receive $12,000 this April, but now could end up with nothing.

"At least with the communists, everyone was poor but everyone could feed their families. Now, with the new order, we have been left destitute," said Rroshi, wrapped up against the winter chill in a shabby grey overcoat.

His wooden hut sits on the side of the street and has no running water, just a filthy mattress and one naked light. Pages cut out of a magazine showing pictures of Persian rugs are stuck to the window and act as makeshift curtains.
The rent is $60 a month while his state pension is just $40. He tries to make up the difference with odd jobs but fears he will soon lose his cherished independence.
"I can't afford to carry on here and will end up in the old men's poor house," he said.
As a young man under Europe's most repressive communist regime, Rroshi quickly became known as a troublemaker, attacking the Stalinist party for seizing family land.
He wanted to be a sculptor, but was kicked out of art school after just a year because of his continued criticism of the political system.

He took up welding, but in 1957 was hauled before the courts and sentenced to four years in jail for political dissent. Between then and 1987 he was in and out of jail, spending 19 years in Albania's feared and filthy prisons.

He still has all the court statements which document his various trials -- four years for dissent, eight months for attacking a policeman who had called him a reactionary, nine years for spreading propaganda, four years for more dissent and sympathising with the West.
"My hatred of the system grew worse after the first jail term. I wasn't ready to sit back and keep quiet," he said.

In all, 34,135 people were imprisoned during more than four decades of communist rule in a country which now has a population of 3.4 million. A further 59,009 people were sent into internal exile and 5,487 executed.
"They were hard years, and when I came out my wife left me, saying the party was now her protector, not me," Rroshi said.
After years of deprivation, the arrival of democracy should have brought an end to his problems, but now he is penniless and bitter, blaming the rightist government for his plight.
"They haven't protected us. They just let these pyramids milk us dry and leave us broke," he said.
